results.proof_sketch: Suppose p zombies guarantee capture within t rounds. Their radius-t neighborhoods must cover every initial survivor vertex: otherwise the survivor starts outside all of them and remains stationary, and no zombie can traverse the initial distance within t moves. An L1-ball of radius t is contained in an L∞ cube of size (2t+1)^k, so n^k≤p(2t+1)^k. Put x=p+t. Since p≤x and 2t+1≤3x, n^k≤3^k x^{k+1}. Hence p+t≥3^{-k/(k+1)}n^{k/(k+1)}. Minimizing over p proves the claim.

results.claim: Mesh capture lemma: for each r≥1 there are constants M_r,A_r such that, on every r-dimensional Cartesian grid with coordinate meshes containing both endpoints and having gaps at most d, placing M_r zombies at every mesh intersection guarantees capture in at most A_r d rounds.
results.proof_sketch: Take M_1=A_1=1. Two consecutive mesh zombies bracketing a survivor on a path form barriers and capture within d rounds. Inductively set M_r=2rM_{r-1} and A_r=(r+1)(A_{r-1}+1). Write R=A_{r-1}d. For each coordinate i choose a lower and upper mesh hyperplane: use the graph boundary if it is within R of the survivor; otherwise choose a mesh hyperplane whose distance is in [R,R+d). On each of these 2r labeled hyperplanes, assign M_{r-1} zombies per mesh point and run the (r−1)-dimensional strategy against the survivor's projection, moving only in the other coordinates. Every prescribed move is a legal shortest-path move in the full grid. Within R rounds some zombie on each hyperplane matches all coordinates except i. The survivor cannot cross a nonboundary hyperplane before then, while a boundary cannot be crossed, so these become lower and upper i-guards. The factor 2r in M_r supplies disjoint teams even at intersecting hyperplanes. Maintain an established guard by repairing the one projected coordinate changed in the preceding survivor move, or, if its projection still matches, advancing in coordinate i. After one extra move all guards are aligned. Let W be the sum, over i, of the separations between the two i-guards. Initially W<2r(R+d). If the survivor changes coordinate j, the j-guards advance and reduce W by 2 while all other guards repair their j-coordinate; if the survivor stays, every pair advances. Crossing or equality causes capture. Thus capture follows within R+1+r(A_{r-1}+1)d≤A_r d rounds.

results.claim: Consequently, for every fixed k≥3, th_z((P_n)^{□k})=Θ_k(n^{k/(k+1)})=Θ_k(|G|^{1/(k+1)}); in particular the k=3 endpoint is complete.
results.proof_sketch: Use the mesh {0,d,2d,…,n−1} in every coordinate. It has at most n/d+2 points per coordinate, so the mesh lemma uses at most M_k(n/d+2)^k zombies and captures within A_kd rounds. Taking d=⌈n^{k/(k+1)}⌉ makes both quantities O_k(n^{k/(k+1)}). Together with the lower bound this proves equality in order. The recurrences give M_3=24 and A_3=28, hence for k=3 one explicit strategy uses at most 24(n/d+2)^3 zombies and capture time at most 28d, with d=⌈n^{3/4}⌉.

final_writeup:
The answer is affirmative for every fixed k≥3.

Let G_{n,k}=(P_n)^{□k}, represented by {0,…,n−1}^k with L1 adjacency. Thus |G_{n,k}|=n^k.

Lower bound. If p zombies have worst-case capture time t, their initial radius-t neighborhoods cover G_{n,k}. Indeed, a survivor outside their union can stay at its initial vertex, which no zombie can reach in t moves. Every radius-t L1-ball contains at most (2t+1)^k vertices, whence

n^k ≤ p(2t+1)^k.

For x=p+t, we have p≤x and 2t+1≤3x, so n^k≤3^k x^{k+1}. Therefore every throttling strategy satisfies

p+t ≥ 3^{-k/(k+1)}n^{k/(k+1)}.

Upper bound. We prove the mesh capture lemma stated above. For each coordinate choose a mesh containing 0 and n−1 whose consecutive gaps are at most d. Define

M_1=A_1=1,   M_r=2rM_{r−1},   A_r=(r+1)(A_{r−1}+1).

Place M_r zombies at every r-dimensional mesh intersection. For r=1, the two consecutive mesh zombies bracketing the survivor capture it within d rounds: the survivor cannot cross either zombie, and their separation decreases each round.

Assume the lemma in dimension r−1 and put R=A_{r−1}d. For every coordinate i, select one mesh hyperplane on either side of the survivor. If the relevant graph boundary is closer than R, use that boundary; otherwise select a hyperplane at distance between R and R+d. On each of these 2r hyperplanes, a disjoint team runs the dimension-(r−1) strategy against the projection of the survivor obtained by deleting coordinate i. These projected moves decrease the full L1 distance and hence are legal zombie moves. Each team obtains, within R rounds, a zombie agreeing with the survivor in every coordinate except i. Before that time the survivor cannot pass a selected hyperplane at initial distance at least R, and it can never pass a graph boundary. The resulting zombie is therefore an i-guard on the correct side. The recurrence M_r=2rM_{r−1} provides disjoint teams even where selected hyperplanes intersect.

Once a guard has matched the survivor's projection, maintain it as follows. If the survivor's preceding move changed a coordinate other than i, the guard repairs that unique mismatch. Otherwise it advances toward the survivor in coordinate i. It consequently remains on its assigned side; attempting to cross it causes capture. After at most one additional round beyond R, there are aligned lower and upper guards for every coordinate.

Let W be the sum of the k separations between corresponding guard pairs. Each selected pair of hyperplanes was separated by less than 2(R+d), so initially W<2r(R+d). If the survivor moves in coordinate j, then on the next zombie turn the two j-guards advance inward, decreasing W by 2, while every other guard repairs its j-coordinate. If the survivor stays, all guard pairs advance. Unless capture has already occurred, W therefore decreases by at least 2 per round. Capture occurs within at most r(A_{r−1}+1)d further rounds. Including the setup phase gives at most

R+1+r(A_{r−1}+1)d ≤ (r+1)(A_{r−1}+1)d=A_rd

rounds, completing the induction.

For G_{n,k}, use the coordinate mesh {0,d,2d,…,n−1}, which has at most n/d+2 points in each coordinate. The strategy therefore uses at most M_k(n/d+2)^k zombies and has capture time at most A_kd. Set d=⌈n^{k/(k+1)}⌉. Since k is fixed, both terms are O_k(n^{k/(k+1)}). For sufficiently large n the number of zombies is at most |G|; the finitely many smaller cases are absorbed by the constant (or handled by initially occupying every vertex).

Thus

th_z(G_{n,k})=Θ_k(n^{k/(k+1)})=Θ_k(|G_{n,k}|^{1/(k+1)}).

For k=3, M_3=24 and A_3=28, yielding the explicit bound th_z(G_{n,3})≤24(n/d+2)^3+28d with d=⌈n^{3/4}⌉.
